planting.note: Pot up nursery starts into a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss, orchid bark, and perlite, and keep conditions humid but airy year-round.

directions: Nepenthes pervillei is the only pitcher plant species found outside Asia, growing wild only on the exposed granite summits of Mahe and Silhouette in the Seychelles. Unlike most jungle-dwelling Nepenthes, it naturally roots directly in thin, nutrient-poor soil pockets on sun-blasted rock faces in cool, misty, wind-swept highland conditions, so it tolerates considerably more direct sun than lowland relatives. It is slow-growing, protected in the wild, and only occasionally offered as seed-grown plants through specialist carnivorous-plant nurseries and society seed banks, so it is best suited to an experienced grower with a terrarium or greenhouse that can hold steady humidity. Water only with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and never fertilize the soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in deep shade to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with year-round high humidity in zone 11-12.

directions: Phoenicophorium borsigianum is a solitary, single-trunk palm endemic to the humid granite forest understory of Mahe, Praslin, and Silhouette in the Seychelles. Young plants carry large, undivided, pleated, diamond-shaped leaves that split irregularly into broad segments with age, an unusual developmental pattern among palms. Its common name 'thief palm' refers to the sharp, saw-toothed margins along the leaf petioles, which locals noted could snag or injure anyone reaching in carelessly. It is grown by specialist tropical palm collectors and botanical gardens in zone 11-12 or large humid greenhouses, demanding deep shade and consistent moisture while young and only tolerating more light once well established.
sources: Dransfield, J. et al. — Genera Palmarum

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil with high year-round humidity in zone 11-12.

directions: Deckenia nobilis is a tall, solitary palm endemic to the upland forests of Mahe in the Seychelles, developing a conspicuous cone of stilt roots at the trunk base and a trunk armored with blackish spines when young. In its homeland it has long been harvested for its edible growing heart, known locally as palmiste or 'millionaire's salad,' though wild harvest is now regulated because of its conservation status. Young plants need steady warmth, high humidity, and deep shade, becoming more sun-tolerant and self-sufficient only after the trunk has formed, which makes this a specialist collector's palm for large tropical greenhouses or frost-free zone 11-12 gardens rather than a casual houseplant.
sources: Dransfield, J. et al. — Genera Palmarum
Seychelles Islands Foundation — Flora of the Seychelles

subcategory: Seychelles endemic small stilt-rooted understory palm

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with high year-round humidity in zone 11-12.

directions: Nephrosperma vanhoutteanum is a slender, solitary understory palm endemic to the shaded granite forests of Mahe, Praslin, and Silhouette in the Seychelles, where it grows beneath the forest canopy alongside the larger Phoenicophorium and Deckenia. It carries a light skirt of small aerial stilt roots at the base and finely divided pinnate leaves on a slim trunk, giving it a more delicate look than its larger relatives. It is a slow-growing, genuinely rare plant found only through specialist rare-palm seed sources, and it needs constant warmth, high humidity, and filtered to deep shade, making it suitable only for a dedicated tropical greenhouse or conservatory rather than outdoor planting outside the warmest frost-free climates.
sources: Dransfield, J. et al. — Genera Palmarum

planting.note: Direct sow in place in early spring, since the deep taproot resents transplanting once established.

directions: Crambe tataria is a large, rounded steppe perennial from the cabbage family, native to the dry grasslands of the Pannonian and Pontic steppe across Hungary, Romania, and Ukraine. Deeply dissected gray-green leaves form a broad basal mound, from which a billowing haze of small white four-petaled flowers rises in early summer, giving a baby's-breath-like effect on a much larger, more architectural scale. A deep taproot makes it exceptionally drought tolerant once established and allows it to persist for decades on lean, fast-draining soil that would rot more demanding perennials. Because it dislikes root disturbance, it is best direct-sown where it is to grow rather than started indoors and transplanted.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in early spring; fresh seed needs a cold period and can take a full season or more to germinate.

directions: Adonis vernalis opens large, glossy, buttercup-yellow flowers in very early spring, often before the surrounding steppe grasses have greened up, above finely dissected, ferny foliage. It is native to dry, calcareous grassland and steppe across the Pannonian basin and the wider Eurasian steppe belt, where it grows on lean, well-drained soil in full sun. All parts of the plant contain cardiac glycosides and are toxic if eaten, so it should be sited away from grazing animals and curious pets. It is slow to establish from seed and resents disturbance once planted, so it is best left undivided for many years in a permanent spot.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in a permanent spot, since mature clumps resent root disturbance and seed germination is slow and erratic.

directions: Dictamnus albus is an upright, long-lived, clump-forming perennial with glossy, lemon-scented compound leaves, topped in late spring with spikes of white, pink-veined, star-shaped flowers. It grows wild across dry grassland and scrub margins of the Pannonian basin and the broader Eurasian steppe-forest transition zone, favoring lean, well-drained, often calcareous soil in full sun. Its common name comes from the flammable volatile oils released by the flowers and ripening seed pods on hot days, historically said to be briefly ignitable with a match, though this is more a curiosity than a reliable garden trick. Once established it can live for decades without division, so choose its permanent site carefully.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant young starts in spring; established tussocks resent being divided or transplanted.

directions: Stipa pennata is a fine-textured tussock grass of the dry Pannonian and Pontic steppe grasslands, where it is a defining species of open, sun-baked, lean soils across the Hungarian puszta and similar landscapes. In early summer each tussock sends up long, silvery-white, feathery awns that can reach nearly a foot in length, catching light and moving dramatically in the slightest breeze. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and performs best when left undisturbed, since mature clumps do not divide or transplant well. The dried awns are also prized for cut and dried arrangements.

planting.note: Plant young potted divisions in early spring and leave undisturbed afterward, since established plants resent transplanting.

directions: Pulsatilla grandis produces large, upright, violet-purple, bell-shaped flowers covered in fine silky hairs in early spring, opening before the finely cut, ferny foliage has fully expanded, followed by decorative silvery, feathery seed heads. It is centered on the dry, calcareous grassland and steppe slopes of the Pannonian basin, distinguishing it from the higher-elevation alpine pasque flowers found in the Carpathians and other mountain ranges. It needs sharply drained, lean soil in full sun and resents being moved once established, so it is best planted young as a division or potted start and then left alone. Established plants are long-lived and slowly form larger clumps over many years.
